about.title: Petaluma Medical Malpractice Claims
about.longDescription: Sonoma County residents rely on a mix of local clinics and larger regional hospitals for care, and most visits go the way they should. But when a diagnosis is missed, a surgery goes wrong, or medication errors cause harm, the aftermath can be confusing and frightening. California's malpractice rules, known as MICRA, add extra layers that don't apply to a typical injury claim — strict notice periods, expert review requirements, and specific damage rules. If you or a family member were harmed during treatment in Petaluma, understanding whether what happened crosses the line from a poor outcome into malpractice usually takes a professional review. LawProactive doesn't practice law itself; we simply connect Petaluma residents with an independent attorney, free of charge, who can review the medical records and explain whether a claim may be worth pursuing. There's no obligation to move forward after that conversation.

whyChoose.title: What Matters Most in a MICRA Claim

items.title: Strict Timing Rules
items.desc: California generally gives one year from when you discover the harm, and no more than three years from the injury itself, so acting sooner rather than later matters.

items.title: Mandatory 90-Day Notice
items.desc: Before a lawsuit can even be filed, California law requires a 90-day notice to the healthcare provider, which needs to be handled correctly and early.

items.title: Expert Review Is Almost Always Required
items.desc: Because a bad medical outcome alone isn't enough to prove malpractice, a qualified medical expert typically has to weigh in on whether the care fell below accepted standards.

items.question: Does a bad outcome from surgery mean malpractice occurred?
items.answer: Not necessarily. California law recognizes that medicine involves risk, so a poor result by itself isn't proof of malpractice. An attorney typically needs a qualified medical expert to review the case and determine whether the care provided fell below the accepted standard.

items.question: How long do I have to bring a claim after treatment in Petaluma?
items.answer: Under MICRA, you generally have one year from when you discover the injury, but no more than three years from when it happened, whichever comes first. There's also a required 90-day notice period before a lawsuit can be filed, so it helps to start the review process well before any deadline gets close.

items.question: Is there a limit on what I can recover for pain and suffering?
items.answer: Yes. California law caps non-economic damages — things like pain and suffering — in medical malpractice cases, though that cap rises annually under current law. Economic damages, such as medical bills and lost income, aren't subject to that same cap.
